summary: Outlines a possible but not recommended method to reduce the effect of collisions in the DNS namespace by giving end users a way to disambiguate the conflict.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7304 describes a way to ask users to choose when a DNS name has conflicting meanings. It warns that the method creates serious usability and security problems and should not be deployed.

questions: what is a dns namespace collision
subtitle: A documented but explicitly discouraged response to DNS name collisions.

tldr.problem: A DNS name can refer to different places in different namespaces, such as an organization's internal name and a public top-level domain.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes looking up the name in multiple namespaces and asking the user which result they intended, through a resolver, application, or proxy.
tldr.outcome: The RFC explicitly does not recommend this approach. A user may not know the right answer, automated systems cannot answer, and the prompt can add delay or expose internal names.

today: RFC 7304 is an Informational document describing an approach that it explicitly says not to implement. It explains the problems with relying on user choice to resolve DNS namespace collisions.

sections.title: How a Namespace Collision Happens
sections.content: A DNS namespace collision can happen when an organization uses a name internally and the same string is delegated as a top-level domain. Someone entering “www.foo” may mean an internal host such as “www.foo.example.com” or the host “www” in the public “foo” domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The same short name can point to an internal host or a public Internet name. The software may not know which one the user means.

sections.title: The User-Choice Method
sections.content: The method described in RFC 7304 checks multiple namespaces. If the lookups conflict, it presents the choices to a user and returns the selected result to the application. The document lists a resolver shim, a replacement resolver, application support, and a proxy interstitial page as possible locations for the prompt.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer checks both places and shows the user the competing results. The user chooses which name to use.

sections.title: Why the RFC Does Not Recommend It
sections.content: The RFC says the method is not recommended. A person may not be available to answer, may not know which result is correct, or may be tricked into choosing the wrong one. The extra interaction can cause delay, and caching a choice can cause problems when a user changes location. The prompt may also reveal internal names.
sections.plainLanguage: People may not know which choice is safe, and automated systems cannot answer. The prompt can also slow requests, reveal internal names, or preserve a choice that becomes wrong elsewhere.
